      S A N F R A N C I S C O B O A R D S A I L I N G A S S O C I AT I O N



The State of Recreational Access to
      The San Francisco Bay:
                          2026




                      Annual Site Access Audit
                         October 2026 · sfba.org
S A N F R A N C I S C O B O A R D S A I L I N G A S S O C I AT I O N



Introduction
October 1, 2026 · Andrew Sullivan, President

During a recent community outreach meeting held by the city of Richmond in collaboration with The
Watershed Project, the project lead, Naama Raz-Yaseef, presented a map showing the impact of sea level rise
flooding that will affect Richmond's shoreline by 2050. This land is largely Bay fill and is home to much of the
city's industry. The main steward of this land is Chevron, and the company is not yet cooperating with the
city's efforts to understand soil toxicity, among other things. Richmond and The Watershed Project are
managing arguably the most professional example of a shoreline planning effort in the region, and attendees at
this community outreach meeting were celebrating the belief that they were ahead of the curve, building
visionary plans to address the environmental challenge of our generation. But as Naama Raz-Yaseef clearly and
precisely reviewed the detailed findings in her measured voice, the 2050 flood map, with its underlying story of
community meetings, design revisions, environmental reviews, construction designs, funding acquisition and
scope changes, was telling a haunting story: we may already be too late and the consequences are going to be
enormous.
This report presents the San Francisco Boardsailing Association's annual audit of site access across the Bay.
Each launch is rated in one of three categories:
    Closed: the public cannot legally or physically reach the water to launch.
    Compromised: the site is open, but access is already reduced by lost parking, restricted hours, erosion,
    riprap or failing facilities.
    Threatened: access is adequate today, but a pending decision, project or ongoing erosion is likely to reduce
    or end it. "Mid-term" marks threats expected beyond the next few years.
A site can be both compromised and threatened.
2026 has been a dynamic year, and the nature of the risk has shifted sharply since our 2025 audit. Last year's
findings centered on erosion and operational neglect, conditions that degrade access gradually and can often
be reversed. This year the threat is different: decisions now before regulators and local agencies will set access
terms for decades. Two forces are driving most of that change, and they put some sites at risk of being lost
outright.
Public land, put to private use. The largest threat in this report is the strong trend to use public land for
private use and revenue. Berkeley is the most serious case. The city is seeking a BCDC permit to charge for
parking on land filled for public recreation, and it has proposed converting a significant part of its recreational
waterfront into a parking lot for a ferry terminal. BCDC will rule on the first step in this process, a permit to
charge for parking, in the coming months. Treasure Island is next. San Francisco was allowed to build housing
there in exchange for committing the shoreline to public use, yet it still plans a visitor toll and has approved
parking meters on both islands. If either city succeeds, it wil provide every agency that holds shoreline land a
template to monetize our parks.
Erosion, and how we respond to it. At 3rd Avenue, Crown Beach, Toll Plaza, Ocean Beach, Crissy Field and
Candlestick, the beach itself is at stake, for different reasons:
    3rd Avenue: the upper launch has been washing away for more than a decade, and Foster City's new levee
    protects the city, not the sand in front of it.
    Crown Beach: there is "almost no beach left" near the concession, and emergency rock is being stockpiled
    for this winter's storms.
    Toll Plaza: already closed by the Port, and now inside a sea level rise plan built around protecting the Bay
    Bridge toll plaza, with no commitment yet to preserving the beach or improving access to it.
    Ocean Beach: losing sand while sand is mined from the Bay and sold.




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                         Page 1
    Crissy Field: the launch lot floods at 3 feet of sea level rise, and the plan to adapt it could change the layout
    that makes the launch work.
    Candlestick: recurring flooding and lost parking.
The usual response to erosion is rock and walls. They protect what sits behind the beach, but the beach is lost.
Without designs and funding in place before the first floods, rock and walls will be the default. But these
designs don't take a critical factor into account: as the Bay rises, it pushes shoreline groundwater up with it.
The rising water reaches contaminated soils that have stayed dry for decades. Salt in the water loosens metals
bound in those soils, and the groundwater carries the pollutants back into the Bay. Seawalls and levees don't
necessarily address this. More than 1,500 contaminated sites around the Bay could be exposed with one meter
of sea level rise, and many of these are located around our most popular launches.
The work itself can be a barrier. Resilient shoreline planning can cost access in three ways:
    Construction closes launches. Shoreline projects take years to build, and sites often close while they are
    built: South Ocean Beach is expected to close for about six months of every year during construction. Even
    projects that stay out of the water take parking for staging. With projects under way around the entire Bay,
    sailors could lose launches in several places at once, for years at a time.
    The clock is shorter than it looks. 2050 sounds far off. It isn't. Shoreline projects can take decades to plan,
    permit, fund and build, so the designs that will meet the first floods are being decided now. As we have seen
    with Foster City and Alameda, emergency response means riprap.
    Everyone will need the same people at once. Every city on the Bay, and coastal communities across the
    state, the country and the world, will be competing for funding, engineers, contractors and equipment. We
    have already what this might mean at 3rd Avenue, when access was compromised for an extended period
    because the crews and equipment needed to fix a large pole at the neighboring golf course were tied up
    rebuilding golf courses damaged in the Los Angeles fires. Think about how this competing demand for
    resources on a Bay-wide, regional, state and national level might affect our ability to implement complex
    and costly solutions.
Both forces play out against a larger need to rethink our shoreline. The same long-term planning that threatens
access is also the opportunity: a new park at Golden Gate Fields, the SFBA's study at 3rd Avenue (part of a
larger effort to create a resilient shoreline there) and Crissy Field Next can each be designed with water access
built in, if recreation is in the record before the designs are drawn.
The roughly 5,000 boardsailors we represent depend primarily on four keystone launches: Alameda, 3rd
Avenue, Berkeley, and Crissy. Three of those four face binding decisions within the next twelve months. Nearly
every inch of our shoreline is currently under initial phases of long-term but critical shoreline planning. The
volume and permanence of change arriving at once is without precedent in the Association's history, and it is
the reason this year's audit warrants closer attention than most.
How you can help. Join or renew your SFBA membership at sfba.org. Your dues help support our work. Then
get involved where you sail. Every site in this report has a plan, a hearing or a decision coming up, listed in the
priorities and links at the end of each section. Comment, show up, and tell us what you see on the water. The
agencies writing these plans need to hear from the people who use the shoreline, and they need to hear it
before the designs are finalized. We urge you to get involved in the SFBA now.

QQberkeleyQQ




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                                    Page 5
QQberkeleyQQ




                                                                         Berkeley Marina
                                                                         COMPROMISED · THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         BCDC parking hearing, “in the coming months”


Berkeley is the most serious threat in this report, both for the access it would take away and for the
precedent it would set.
The city filled the Bay in the 1960s to build a regional park, and asked for state and federal recreation
money to build it. It now wants to charge for parking in the lots that serve the South Basin launches, and
to give part of its waterfront to a commuter ferry terminal. It points to a shortfall in the marina fund to
justify both. If the BCDC allows Berkeley to put a price on access to land filled for public recreation,
every East Bay shoreline park becomes a potential source of revenue. At stake is whether a city can take
land on public terms, then rewrite those terms and sidestep the regulators who enforce them. The
answer will decide not only who can afford to reach the shore but also what purpose our shoreline
serves.
Where SFBA stands. SFBA does not oppose ferries or development at the waterfront. We oppose paying
for them with access to one of the few places on the Bay where people can launch, swim, wade, fish, sail
and simply enjoy our shoreline. Put the terminal inside the marina, not out in the Bay. Be honest about
what it costs, who it serves and how riders get there: most of them drive, and every one who drives
needs a parking space.
The two proposals.
          Paid parking. Berkeley's city parking programs lost $1.55M in FY2025 ($4.93M in revenue against
          $6.48M in costs). And without any supporting details, Berkeley claims that paid parking in the marina
          will generate $182,000 a year, which they claim is essential for maintaining boating facilities. But at the
          same time, the city is sliding more than $2 million in boating revenues out the side door instead of
          maintaining boating facilities. In their proposal, 273 spaces at South Cove and the South Basin would
          become paid parking at $6 a day or $500 a year. Four 10-minute loading zones would take out 4 more
          spaces. Furthermore, the city can change the program at any time, a trial can become permanent
          administratively, and monitoring would be staff observation only. BCDC has made paid parking a
          major permit. It is off the October 15 agenda and is "anticipated … in the coming months" (BCDC,
          September 30, 2026). Does this look like a city acting in the best interest of its park users?
          The pier-ferry terminal. A 1,080-foot pier and a 400-foot breakwater, with 275 spaces in existing
          waterfront lots converted to paid, full-day parking for ferry riders (200 on Seawall Drive, 75 at
          Skates/North). While the city puts the cost at $174M, we estimate over $200M, against about $300M
          available for all new ferry capital in the region. The Draft EIR comment period closed April 28. On




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                  Page 6
    September 16 the Governor certified the project for SB 149 fast-tracked court review. A Final EIR, a
    council vote and a BCDC permit are still ahead, but the city has already moved to seek $25M from
    MTC for landside work.

The city's revised parking application says that without the projected parking revenue it cannot fix a
broken hoist and a sinkhole by the failed seawall at South Cove. It concedes that fewer users can launch
sailboats as a result.
How the marina fund was drained. The city claims that changes need to be made to address a chronic
deficit at the Marina. Jim McGrath's review of city budgets since 2000, however, points to a deficit
largely of the city's own making:
    Since FY2001: at least $18M in waterfront park maintenance and recreation programs has been
    charged to the marina fund instead of the parks tax, including more than $2M in FY2025 alone.
    Parks taxes: a 2014 increase has raised more than $20M, and a 2024 measure earmarked for the
    waterfront parks has raised about $3M. None of the 2014 money has gone to marina facilities.
    2022–2026: about $13M in Coastal Conservancy grants went to things other than asset repair,
    including ferry-terminal development.
    Failures: the pier closed in 2015. East Dock closed in February 2025 and was lost for about half the
    season. It was built, and later rebuilt, mostly with grants Berkeley accepted along with an agreement
    to maintain it.

The neglect has its own cost. About 200 berths sit vacant, losing roughly $300,000 a year, and there is
no reserve for dredging. In September 2026 the city tied South Cove repairs to approval of paid parking.

What Berkeley promised, and what the law requires.
    A park built with public money. In its 1965 application to BCDC, Berkeley described the South Basin
    as a "131-acre Marine Park" and sought federal Land and Water Conservation Fund money for it.
    Recent Bay Trail, parking, restroom and dock improvements serving the lots now targeted for fees
    cost about $18.6M, much of it from state and regional grants.
    Bay Plan Recreation Policy 3. Recreational facilities should be "easily available from parking reserved
    for the public," and launch sites for non-motorized boats need "sufficient, convenient parking that
    accommodates expected use." The city's answer, free parking up to a third of a mile away, does not
    work for anyone carrying a sail, a kayak or a wing.
    Recreation Policy 9. Ferry parking "should not be usurped" from park and marina users.
    Equity. BCDC guidance says public access to the Bay should "in general" be free of charge. More than
    10% of respondents to the city's own survey report household income of $25,000, and apart from one
    council hearing, the city has done none of the outreach BCDC's environmental justice policies call for.
    Public trust. The marina sits on tidelands granted in trust. The city must account for trust revenues
    to the State Lands Commission (Public Resources Code §6306), and the state Constitution says access
    to navigable waters "shall be always attainable for the people."

There is not enough parking for both. The city's consultants forecast about 915 ferry riders a day. At
WETA's existing terminals, 48% of riders drive and park, and the city's own consultants put it at 55–60%.
That is roughly 440 to 550 cars a day. The plan provides 265 paid, time-limited spaces and sends the rest




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                  Page 7
to Marina Boulevard and University Avenue. Meanwhile about 171,000 people a year visit the south
waterfront, around 470 a day, many driving because they carry gear or kids. Both groups would compete
for the same lots on the same days.
The city's count is built to come out low. It rests on five days of counts in 2024, taken on weekends, off-
season or at 4 p.m., after the midday peak. Even so, the consultant counted 67 cars on Seawall Drive at
peak, where the city now proposes 33 spaces. The baseline is also a low point: a pier closed since 2015, a
failed dock and a silted basin. Racetrack, EBRPD's Albany Beach, shows what happens when shoreline
access is improved: after EBRPD's 2020 rebuild, use jumped. BCDC has asked the city for real data on
recreational demand. Anonymized mobility data can provide it, but the city refuses to use it, because
those numbers tell a story the city doesn't want to tell.
Who gets pushed out. The south waterfront lots serve the activities that need gear and a nearby car:
76% of sailing and boating visits, 75% of playground visits and 70% of swimming visits in the city's own
survey. They also serve more lower-income visitors: 20% of south-lot respondents earn under $75,000,
against 8% in the north. In San Diego, paid parking at Balboa Park cut visits by 34%. The city's agreement
with WETA promises ferry riders parking "within a reasonable distance." Recreational users deserve the
same standard.
Who has authority over the waterfront. Berkeley argues that BCDC can only review the 53 of 273 spaces
within 100 feet of the shoreline. BCDC's own ferry staff report says jurisdiction south of University
Avenue "is difficult to confirm." Jim McGrath, a former BCDC commissioner, went back to the original
documents:
    BCDC permitted the fill itself. Permit 1966.028.00 approved 4.6 acres of fill for "a marina restaurant,
    public beach, park area, automobile parking, and a relocated and expanded University of California
    sailing facility." It has never been amended.
    The fill came after the McAteer-Petris Act. When BCDC's jurisdiction began, the city had paid only
    for the containment dike, not the fill behind it. The South Basin was brought to its current elevation
    afterward, and Berkeley never obtained a vested-right exemption.
    A designated priority recreation area. The Bay Plan marks the waterfront as Waterfront Park/Beach
    Priority Use Area #48.

The city has also split the project into four pieces reviewed separately: the ferry terminal, paid parking,
spaces set aside for a restaurant tenant, and a Waterfront Specific Plan that could triple commercial
space. BCDC should set its jurisdiction from the permit record, not the city's map, and review the four
pieces as one project.
What the city's analysis leaves out. BCDC's comments on the ferry Draft EIR asked for "additional
details regarding existing demand for recreational facilities" and said the DEIR rejects the in-Marina
location but "does not adequately explain why."

    The most expensive way to move a commuter. WETA spends about $28.80 per ride and collects $5.40
    in fares, a subsidy of roughly $23 every trip (Paul Kamen, from WETA's FY2024–25 budget). The
    regional money covering that gap is expected to run out around 2030, and Berkeley pays for the
    landside facilities.
    The in-marina alternative. The terminal was originally planned inside the marina. McGrath estimates
    the location out in the Bay saves about four minutes, at a cost of $170–205M, leaving Berkeley with a
    bill of at least $40M. Alameda's Seaplane Lagoon terminal cost $23M, and Paul Kamen has sketched an



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                   Page 8
             in-marina design at about $20M. The city has not produced a costed in-marina alternative.

Why it matters beyond Berkeley. Windsurfers, wingers, kayakers, swimmers, Cal Sailing Club, Cal
Adventures, anglers and all sorts of shoreline visitors use these lots, and fees fall hardest on those who
live beyond biking distance. Berkeley is one of four launches most of the Bay's boardsailors depend on,
and the East Bay's other options are shrinking: Toll Plaza is gated, Crown Beach is squeezed by riprap,
parking at Point Isabel will tighten during the park's 2027 cap project and, due to improvements there,
and it's often difficult to park at Racetrack. By the city's own account this would be BCDC's first
standalone permit for parking fees. Approving it would give every city and agency a template: divert the
maintenance money, let the facilities fail, then charge the public to fix them. TIDA is already following
the same pattern at Treasure Island. This is a disturbing trend to commercialize our shoreline parks.
If Berkeley is permitted to meter recreational parking at the South Basin, it will disrupt the largest
source of shoreline recreational parking in the East Bay and one of the largest in our region. We have a
house-of-cards of local access, so shoreline decisions must be made with a strong eye for regional
implications. In order to do this, we must have an accurate understanding of parking demand and plans
that address it.
2026–27 priorities:

             Seek denial of the paid parking permit. If anything is approved, it should be a time-limited trial with a
             sunset date, independent monitoring and a use baseline reconstructed from mobility data, and it must
             not become permanent administratively.
             Ask BCDC to review the parking fees and the ferry parking plan as one project.
             Set the baseline with real data, using mobility data and the Racetrack comparison, to answer BCDC's
             request for data on recreational demand.
             Require the full §6306 trust accounting, and fund the East Dock and South Cove repairs before any
             fee.
             Hold off on ferry funding, including the $25M MTC request, until there is a Final EIR, a BCDC permit, a
             full cost estimate, a revised MOU and a costed in-marina alternative.
             No net loss of recreational parking, measured at peak recreational hours with an understanding of
             latent demand.

Next decisions: the BCDC paid-parking hearing (expected in the coming months); Berkeley's November 3
bond measure, which includes dock pile replacement; the ferry Final EIR and council vote; and MTC's
decision on the $25M request.
Plans and documents: City of Berkeley, Pier-Ferry project · Waterfront Specific Plan update, Mar 2023 ·
BCDC Design Review Board staff report, Pier-Ferry · BCDC comments on the Draft EIR · Berkeley
Waterfront Community Coalition (parking and TDM reports) · BCDC, San Francisco Bay Plan




QQalbanyQQ




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                           Page 9
QQalbanyQQ




                                                                         Golden Gate Fields and
                                                                         Racetrack
                                                                         THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         EBRPD board vote on purchase agreement, Oct 20, 2026


The largest shoreline land deal in a generation is under way next to one of the Bay's best kite launches.
Golden Gate Fields closed to racing in June 2024. In February 2026 the Trust for Public Land (TPL) took
an option to buy the 161-acre property for $175 million, including removal of the above-ground
structures. Of the 161 acres, about 31 are open water along the shoreline. Roughly 40 acres are in
Berkeley and the rest are in Albany. Here's a snapshot of the funding:

             State: $125 million from the Prop 4 climate bond, through AB 113, signed in September 2026. The site
             must be used principally for parks and open space.
             EBRPD: $20 million from Measure WW.
             TPL: about $30 million from private donors. EBRPD's general manager says the purchase must be
             complete by the end of 2026.

EBRPD will own and manage the park. It expects to take title in spring 2027, run a public planning
process from 2027 to 2029, and build in phases after that as funding allows. The EBRPD board is
scheduled to vote on the purchase agreement on October 20, 2026.
What the plans say so far. The EBRPD and TPL describe trails, habitat and an unbroken shoreline park
from Richmond to Oakland. Neither mentions launches, rigging areas or parking. The only parking
statement on record came from EBRPD's general manager at Albany's September 28 town hall about
folding more parking into Racetrack in phases. At the same meeting, residents proposed paid parking to
replace the revenue the racetrack paid Albany, about $1.1 million a year to the city and $700,000 to the
school district.
The Recreational Ecosystem. Albany's own General Plan supports water access. Policy W-3.5 directs the
city to "designate areas to provide water access for windsurfers, kayakers, and other non-motorized
watercraft." Policy W-3.4 says parking should be "based on actual use patterns," but we've seen a
decrease in boardsailor use due to limited parking. More public access to the shoreline does not
guarantee access to the water, however, so this has to be in the planning record before the landscape is
designed. The introduction of the Bay Trail from Gilman to Buchanan displaced scores of informally
parked cars. Shoreline improvements have increased demand. The significant loss of recreational
parking at Berkeley will have major impacts throughout all of these already stressed East Bay shoreline
parks. With Berkeley moving to paid parking, Toll Plaza closed, Crown Beach losing sand, Point Isabel's
parking squeezed during construction, Racetrack at capacity and Marina Bay short on space, EBRPD's
plans for Golden Gate Fields should be sized for these regional dynamics in mind.

2026–27 priorities:



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                          Page 10
            Ask EBRPD to map launch and landing zones, rigging areas, loading zones and long-duration parking
            within a short carry of the water, and to keep launch corridors clear of fences, posts and plantings.
            Keep interim access to the Golden Gate Fields lots at Racetrack and Fleming Point through the
            transition, with parking of at least three hours.
            Measure current use at Racetrack, Point Isabel and Marina Bay with mobility data before planning
            starts in 2027.
            Oppose paid parking as a way to replace Albany's lost racetrack revenue.
            Secure an SFBA seat in EBRPD's 2027–29 planning process.

Plans and documents: EBRPD, Future Golden Gate Fields Park · Trust for Public Land, Golden Gate
Fields · Albany 2035 General Plan, Waterfront Element · Draft Bay Area Boardsailing Plan, 2019 · Water
Trail, Albany Beach site report




QQcrownQQ




                                                                         Crown Beach, Alameda
                                                                         COMPROMISED · THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         EBRPD–Alameda winter storm plan


On September 27, 2026, Jane Cormier of Boardsports California reported to the SFBA that there was "
almost no beach left" near the concession. EBRPD staff pushed the remaining sand into temporary
ramps, which Jane called "a band aid for the bigger problem." The emergency riprap placed after the
December 2024 storm saved the concession building but left "very limited water access." Crown Beach is
an artificial beach with no natural supply of sand. It survives only when people put sand back. The site is
not only critical for development and learning in the boardsports community, it is a regional destination
for beachgoers with incredibly diverse interests in shoreline access. The lack of commitment to
managing this resource is disrupting use and compromising safety. This pattern of triage management
goes back decades:
            1981–82: An Army Corps study found the beach receding three to seven feet a year. By 1982 it was
            dangerously eroded. A barge pumped Bay sand back onto it, and groins were installed.
            January 2006: A major storm stripped the beach again.
            2013: The last major sand placement. EBRPD pumped 82,600 cubic yards of sand from a barge onto
            the beach, paid for with about $2.5 million from FEMA, State Boating and Waterways and Fish and
            Wildlife. A year earlier, the regional Adapting to Rising Tides assessment had warned that losing the
            beach would cut off boardsailing and other water access, and called it "a significant loss to the
            Alameda community and the entire Bay Area."




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                         Page 11
    Since 2013: Maintenance has meant moving the sand that remains from the ends of the beach back to
    the middle. No new sand has arrived.
    July 2021: Boardsports warned that the kite launch was nearly gone, with a drop of three to four feet
    to the water. That spring's sand redistribution had been smaller than usual.
    January 2022: A rock wall in front of the concession cut off windsports access. "We have literally lost
    our access," Boardsports wrote on January 27. Two days earlier it had sent EBRPD a plan. Short term:
    move the kite launch north of the concession, add two 15-foot ramps at each launch, plus signage,
    snow fencing and sand. Long term: a large sand placement, removing the rock wall, and four
    permanent ramps.
    Since 2022: Those requests have gone largely unmet.
    December 2024: After a winter storm, emergency riprap approved by BCDC was placed in front of the
    concession. It saved the building but left "very limited water access."
    2025: After winter storms, EBRPD trucked in boulders to stabilize the shoreline and the lagoon pump,
    and moved eroded sand back with earthmoving equipment. Alameda's $6.3 million application for
    80,000 cubic yards of South Shore sand went unfunded.
    September 2026: There is "almost no beach left" near the concession. Staff pushed the remaining sand
    into temporary ramps, and rock is being stockpiled for this winter.

Each response has saved a structure or bought a season. None has replaced the sand from the 2013
project, and each round of emergency rock dumping leaves less beach to launch from.

This winter EBRPD and the City of Alameda are planning their storm-surge response, which once again
includes stockpiling rock for emergency repairs. Unless access is designed in, more rock will mean less
beach. Alameda's 2025 application for South Shore sand replenishment ($6.3M project, 80,000 cubic
yards of sand) went unfunded. The city's broader Shoreline Adaptation Plan is due in 2027. EBRPD's
McKay Avenue expansion has no implementation timeline. In short, without access-oriented interim
solutions and a commitment to beach maintenance, this unique gem in our shoreline risks being erased
in an el Nino storm surge this winter.
Another important note that shoreline plans for Alameda and other sites highlight is how solutions to
one problem often cause another. Shoreline design proposals rely heavily on natural offshore features,
such as eel grass, to mitigate tidal and wave energy. But as our sport migrates increasingly to foiling,
these solutions also affect usability. Where and how such wave energy mitigation efforts are
implemented around our limited access points may further compromise our access.
EBRPD leadership changes relevant to Alameda:
    Robert Deikman became Shoreline Unit Manager in August 2026.
    Amy Wooldridge, formerly Alameda's Assistant City Manager, became Deputy General Manager on
    August 31.
    Kirsten Holder, from GGNRA planning, became Assistant General Manager for Acquisition,
    Stewardship and Planning on September 8.

2026–27 priorities:
    Take part in the EBRPD–Alameda winter storm planning.
    Make any further emergency rock come with a defined access route.
    Advocate for permanent ramps and sand before the April wind season.



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                 Page 12
           Build the beginner beach into the South Shore and Shoreline Adaptation plans as an explicit design
           requirement.

Plans and documents: City of Alameda, South Shore Adaptation Project · BCDC, local sea level rise plans
(SB 272)




QQtollQQ




                                                                         Toll Plaza / Radio Beach
                                                                         CLOSED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         BCDC enforcement outcome


The Port of Oakland's gate on the only access road remains in place, with no plan to reopen. Before it
closed, the site regularly drew 30 or more boardsailors and 80 or more users at a time. This was an
important early season site and a reliable launch in winter northerlies. It is also a missing link between
Treasure Island and the East Bay and could be a great beach destination for the region.
In February 2026, BCDC's enforcement staff told the SFBA that BCDC has an enforcement case against
the Port. The case concerns unpermitted fill (trash) within the 100-foot shoreline band at Toll Plaza. Staff
are also "exploring a potential violation involving the lack of public access." According to BCDC, the Port
claims the beach is designated for cell infrastructure and calls the public's use of it trespassing.
A correction to the 2025 audit. BCDC staff noted that the earlier fines were for the McAteer-Petris Act
violation, meaning the trash. They were not for failing to remove the encampment. BCDC has no
authority to remove people.
What the plans say about Toll Plaza. The beach, called Radio Beach in park and planning documents, has
been in regional plans for more than a decade, and recreation was once part of them.
           Gateway Park. Gateway Park is the regional park planned for the foot of the new East Span. The
           partner agencies were the Bay Area Toll Authority, Caltrans, the Port, the East Bay Regional Park
           District and others. The 2013 scoping plans drew Radio Beach with a sandy beach, restoration
           planting, a levee trail, limited parking, and windsurfing as a listed use. A new trail was to run from Key
           Point under the bridge to the beach's north end. The later park plan calls Radio Beach a "restoration
           and preservation area," with interpretive trails, sandy beaches and "fencing to protect wildlife." The
           Draft EIR in January 2018 found significant, unavoidable impacts to biological resources. Only the part
           south of the bridge was built: the 22-acre Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline opened in October
           2020, with the Bridge Yard building and a 600-foot pier on the old bridge's piles. The Radio Beach
           section, the only part of the park north of I-80, was never built.




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                          Page 13
    East Bay Crescent. Emeryville, Berkeley, Albany, Caltrans, EBRPD, the Port and EBMUD are preparing
    a subregional sea level rise plan, led by the SF Estuary Partnership. Its community visioning work ran
    from May 2025 to July 2026 and describes Radio Beach as a "bayfront beach with limited access on the
    north side of the Bay Bridge approach." Two nature-based measures are under study to protect the
    bridge touchdown: a horizontal levee along the Crescent, and placing Port of Oakland dredged
    sediment offshore as a "feeder mound" that slowly supplies the marsh. An Ocean Protection Council
    grant awarded in April 2026 now funds the plan. Either measure could build a beach or bury one.
    Nothing in the record yet says which.
    Caltrans Bay Bridge study. Caltrans District 4 has begun a sea level rise adaptation study for the Bay
    Bridge and the roads and shoreline around its East Bay touchdown, including West Oakland and
    Emeryville. Public workshops began in October 2026, with focus groups and a shoreline site visit to
    follow. Caltrans says it wants to know how people reach the area. Toll Plaza sits at the bridge
    touchdown, so this study could decide whether the beach comes back as access or is armored for the
    bridge.
    The marsh next door. The Emeryville Crescent State Marine Reserve covers about 103 acres from the
    bridge approach to the foot of Powell Street. EBRPD manages it as part of Eastshore State Park.

Toll Plaza is an overlooked and undervalued recreational site, and sits beside a bike corridor that is being
finished in pieces. It is not hard to imagine this site literally being left off the map:
    The Bay Bridge Trail runs more than four miles from Emeryville past the toll plaza to Yerba Buena
    Island.
    The West Oakland Link is an elevated bike and pedestrian path along the south side of West Grand
    Avenue, connecting Mandela Parkway to the bridge path over the rail yards and port truck routes. The
    $63 million interim phase is fully funded: construction starts in 2027 and it should open in 2029. The
    full project, more than $100 million, is targeted for 2031 but has no funding yet.
    The Yerba Buena Island path to Treasure Island is under construction, due in 2028.
    The West Span path to San Francisco is in early planning and unfunded, and could open in 2034 at the
    earliest.

Within a few years, someone could ride from West Oakland past Toll Plaza to Treasure Island, ending at
the island's northeast corner, the launch the island's development agreement committed to improve. Toll
Plaza and Treasure Island would become stops on one continuous route. Toll Plaza would be the only
boardsports beach in Oakland reachable by bike and it would serve families in West Oakland, a
neighborhood cut off from its own shoreline by freeways, rail yards and the Port. Running the Bay Trail
along the Emeryville Crescent to Toll Plaza and then to the bridge is the best way to serve the general
public and align with the Bay Trail mission.
Balancing uses. The Crescent is valued by birders, and the park plan's wildlife fencing reflects that.
Sailors need sand and a clear path to the water, not a marsh. A plan can keep both by re-enforcing a
beach that sticks while protecting habitat with zoned or seasonal limits elsewhere. The SFBA would like
to work out that plan with the birding community rather than against it.
2026–27 priorities:
    Support BCDC's public-access enforcement inquiry and press the Port to reopen the road.
    Ask BATA, EBRPD and the Port to finish the Radio Beach part of Gateway Park, with the water access
    shown in the 2013 plans.



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                 Page 14
         Ask that the West Oakland Link and Yerba Buena Island path plans include a bike connection to Toll
         Plaza, forming one route from West Oakland through Toll Plaza to Treasure Island's northeast corner.
         Make Toll Plaza an explicit access site in the East Bay Crescent plan. Insist that any horizontal levee or
         sediment placement keeps a sandy launch.
         Meet with Golden Gate Bird Alliance and EBRPD on a zoned access plan for the beach and marsh.
         Take part in the Caltrans Bay Bridge study's workshops, focus groups and site visit, and ask that Toll
         Plaza be treated as an access site and a link in the bridge's Bay Trail connections.
