QQrichmondQQ




                                                                         Richmond shoreline:
                                                                         Marina Bay & Point
                                                                         Isabel
                                                                         THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Community workshop Oct 14, 2026


Richmond is conducting arguably the best community outreach and shoreline-design work around the
Bay. Its Sea Level Rise Adaptation and Resiliency Plan covers 32 miles of shoreline and addresses coastal
flooding, groundwater rise and habitat loss. The Watershed Project is running the project with a grant
from the Ocean Protection Council. In December 2025 BCDC formally recognized it as one of the first
subregional plans under the Regional Shoreline Adaptation Plan. Richmond is ahead of the pack.
Two of the East Bay's busiest launches. Richmond hosts two launches the region depends on. At Point
Isabel, more than 40 sailors a day launch on a good day, from a small gravel beach behind a rock jetty. In
2018–19 EBRPD rebuilt the launch with a Water Trail grant from the Coastal Conservancy: a 100-foot
accessible ramp, new stairs and a 3,000-square-foot rigging area. It is an excellent example of building
access through riprap. But erosion is already cutting in where the path meets the water, leaving a drop of
two to three feet that is growing quickly. Every launch, however well built, needs a maintenance
program. The park's 98 parking spaces are already frequently at capacity on weekdays, as they serve one
of the busiest off-leash parks in the country. At Marina Bay, 20 or more windsurfers, wingers and kiters
regularly launch from two small beaches, with parking for only 38 cars. Both sit on low, filled shoreline in
a part of the Bay expected to flood early. And both sites are where sailors will go when other East Bay
launches close, reach capacity or start charging. Every space lost at Berkeley, Racetrack, Toll Plaza or
San Quentin adds demand at these two sites.


SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                        Page 15
The problem here is not a lack of vision and planning, it's the timeline. Much of Richmond's shoreline is
industrial land and fill over legacy contamination, and rising groundwater threatens it from below as well
as from the Bay.
    2025 national study. A Nature Communications study identified more than 20 Richmond hazardous
    sites at risk of 1-in-100-year flooding by 2050, including the Chevron refinery and the Zeneca site.
    2026 state report. The Ocean Protection Council report (dated March 2026) estimates that more than
    1,500 active contaminated sites around the Bay could be exposed to flooding from below with one
    meter of sea level rise. Three of its 21 pilot sites are in Richmond: Reaction Products, the Point Molate
    Naval Supply Center and Zeneca Richmond AG Products.
    Zeneca site. Cleanup is already losing ground. Vapor extraction removed 2 pounds of contaminants in
    2024, and the temporary cap has outlived its design life.

As mentioned in the introduction, the largest shoreline landowner, Chevron, has not been a cooperative
partner. Without the refinery's participation, the plan cannot deal with the most contaminated shoreline
before it floods. If toxins leach into the Bay, water contact anywhere nearby becomes a health question,
and that would close access more completely than any gate. The 2050 flooding implications in Richmond
showcase the often overlooked side-affect of sea level rise: it also pushes water tables up into soils with
high concentrations of toxins, which will leech into the Bay.
Adaptation can close a launch before the water does. Shoreline projects take years to build, and access
shrinks or disapears while they are built. Point Isabel shows how this plays out, even where the launch
itself is spared. EBRPD's North Point Isabel cap project, which stabilizes the old landfill cap and adds sea
level rise resilience, may start in spring 2027 and take up to 24 months. The start date is not set. EBRPD
is still waiting on a BCDC permit, National Park Service approval of matching grant funds, and
documentation from USPS of EBRPD's agreement to operate the park. The work will close the park's
northern section, north of the Hoffman Channel. New fencing will keep people and dogs off the northern
shoreline mudflats. Local users expect the small Rydin Road lot to be used for staging, which will tighten
parking for the whole park. And because the project's permits keep the work out of the Bay, it cannot
add even simple access, such as the stairs to the water that local users have asked for. While the launch
opposite Mudpuppy's is not affected this time, larger projects will not be so contained: staging areas take
parking lots, fencing and habitat buffers move people away from the water, and riprap and levees can
replace a beach for good. In Richmond, where much of the shoreline will need protection at about the
same time, construction could take Marina Bay and other launches out of use for years, and the finished
designs may leave no place to launch at all. As dozens of shoreline projects are built over the next three
decades, their schedules and staging need to be planned so that each part of the Bay keeps at least one
working launch with ample access, and each finished design needs a place to get in the water.
2026–27 priorities:
    Keep recreation and water quality at the center of Richmond's plan, with a firm schedule for the
    contaminated shoreline sites.
    Press for Chevron's full participation, through BCDC and the Regional Water Board if necessary.
    Continue to engage and support Richmond's gold-standard for shoreline design and outreach efforts.
    This is the blueprint the rest of the Bay should follow.
    Protect Point Isabel and Marina Bay as recreational access sites, with their launch, rigging and parking
    needs, before design begins.




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                  Page 16
         Ask EBRPD to keep parking available for the Point Isabel launch during the North Point Isabel Park cap
         project, and to repair the erosion where the launch path meets the water and set up a regular
         maintenance program for the launch.

Plans and documents: City of Richmond, Sea Level Rise Adaptation and Resiliency · BCDC, Richmond
subregional plan notice · EBRPD, North Point Isabel Cap Resilience Project · OPC, sea level rise and
contaminated sites, 2026 · Richmondside, Point Isabel partial closure, Oct 22, 2025 · Water Trail, Point
Isabel site report, 2016 · Draft Bay Area Boardsailing Plan, 2019




QQtiQQ




                                                                         Treasure Island
                                                                         COMPROMISED · THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Unit-increase approval and EIR addendum, end of 2026


Treasure Island has some of the best wind and swell in the Bay, and it is becoming a reliable reliable
options as heat bubbles form over our mainland shoreline. Windsurfers have sailed it for 40 years, and
winging has opened it to a new group of advanced riders. The access we have there was part of a deal
the SFBA supported, but the city is chipping away at its responsibilities to deliver.

The deal terms. San Francisco could not build housing on Treasure Island without clearing the state's
public trust claim to the filled land. The 2004 Treasure Island Public Trust Exchange Act and the title
settlement the State Lands Commission approved in 2012 and revised in 2014 governed the trade:
         About 150 acres were freed from the trust for development.
         In exchange, about 285 acres of upland, and about 850 acres counting tidelands, were committed to
         the public trust for recreation, open space and waterfront uses.
         The Act states that "nothing in this act may be construed to authorize the development of housing on
         trust lands." The settlement requires a pedestrian and bicycle corridor around the shoreline and
         public road access to the eastern and western shores.

The northeast corner was part of the deal. For 40 years, the boat ramp at the island's northeast corner,
at the end of Avenue I, has been where windsurfers, wingers and a few 'brave' kiters launch. The state
didn't just free land for housing. It required the city to keep the north end accessible to recreation. The
title settlement promises "vehicular access to and along the eastern and western shores to the proposed
recreational resources and wetlands at the north end of the island," and requires "adequate access from
the public streets to the Public Trust Lands." BCDC's 2016 permit requires about 54.5 acres of public
access along the shoreline and lists the Northern Shoreline Park boat ramp among the improvements.
The project's environmental review counted windsurfing as an existing use of the island, part of the



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                          Page 17
baseline the project was meant to protect. That review also promised that "visitors to the Islands… would
not be charged a congestion pricing fee." The SFBA supported the handoff with the understanding that
access at the northeast corner would be improved, not rationed.
What the city has done since.

    The toll. The county transportation authority still plans to charge island visitors up to $5 at peak
    hours, with residents exempt. In 2021 the SFBA brought the city's intentions to BCDC. BCDC told the
    city that a toll could affect the public access required by its permit and would need a permit
    amendment. The city paused the toll initiative. The authority's program page lists the start as "TBD,"
    and its 2025–26 work is limited to updating the federal environmental clearance. A $20 million federal
    grant tied to the program was cancelled in May 2025. While stalled, the toll has not been dropped.
    Paid parking. In March 2026 the SFMTA board approved parking meters across both islands: $1 an
    hour to start, set by demand, from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. every day. The agency's stated reason was the new
    open space "drawing more visitors." What the toll has not done, meters may do. Visitors to the
    shoreline will pay to park.
    The NE ramp gate. In March 2025 a security contractor began locking the gate to the NE ramp, the
    main boardsailing launch, at 5 p.m. The gate had been open for 20 years, and no one told users of the
    change. The SFBA wrote to TIDA and BCDC. BCDC staff found nothing in the permit allowing time
    limits and referred the matter to its compliance staff. TIDA now locks the gate at 'sunset'.
    Trust accounting. The State Lands Commission's records list TIDA's annual trust revenue statements
    for 2023 and 2024 as not submitted.

What the northeast corner needs. Sailors now park where they can. About a dozen cars fit along
Northpoint by the vacant housing to the west, and about ten more fit next to occupied homes. Avenue I
takes the overflow, shared with anglers. Late in the season, when Crissy is fogged in, 15 to 20 vehicles
line Avenue I on weekdays and more on weekends. A large lot just east of Avenue I, built for the old
school, was fenced off during the cleanup and never reopened. As new housing fills in, these informal
arrangements will run into residents. The improvements the deal promised are modest:

    posted access hours that run to dusk, so the gate can't be locked again without notice;
    the fenced lot reopened for recreational parking;
    a rigging area;
    a maintained ramp.

None of these is built yet.
Where things stand. The project is largely on hold:
    Housing. Market-rate construction has stalled. The developer is asking to add 1,400 to 2,800 housing
    units because its financing depends on selling homes, not renting them. That change needs an
    environmental review addendum and Board of Supervisors approval, targeted for the end of 2026.
    Parks.
    The first six acres of the western shoreline park opened in September 2025.
    Clipper Cove Park, with beach access and a small parking lot, is expected this year.
    Rec & Park takes over park maintenance from TIDA starting this fiscal year.
    Clipper Cove. The marina rebuild and the paused sailing center are moving on their own track.
    Neither affects the northeast launch.



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                               Page 18
           Leadership. Longtime TIDA director Bob Beck retired in January 2026. Sheela Jivan took over in June.

Why it matters beyond Treasure Island. The Bay Plan is unusually specific about Treasure Island. When
the Navy left, the island was to be redeveloped "for public use," with "continuous public access to the
Bay" and "parking and water access for users of non-motorized small boats, including at north end of the
Island" (Plan Map 4, p. 120). The plan's general policies say the same: sites improved for launching small
boats need "sufficient, convenient parking that accommodates expected use" (Recreation Policy 3.e.(3), p.
72), because places to park "for more than short periods of time" are "needed to provide the public with
full access to the Bay" (Recreation finding p, p. 69).

San Francisco is moving the other way. SFMTA approved paid parking on both islands in March 2026,
while the northeast corner still lacks the launch improvements the development deal promised. Meters
placed more than 100 feet from the water fall outside BCDC's permit jurisdiction, so a city can price
people off the shoreline without BCDC review, unless BCDC treats the parking that makes public access
usable as part of that access. Meters and tolls are forms of regressive taxation, of course, and the burden
falls hardest on those with the least, against the Bay Plan's call for "more equitable and convenient public
access" (Public Access finding h, p. 76).
Treasure Island and Berkeley follow the same pattern. Land was filled or freed for public use under state
trust and BCDC guidelines. The city then backtracks on agreements and looks to monetize the people
that land was meant to serve, through a toll, meters, parking fees and other forms of commercial
development of our parks. If either city succeeds, it paves a way through BCDC authority for all to follow.
2026–27 priorities:
           Get the northeast corner improvements into the next phase of the development agreement: posted
           dawn-to-dusk access, the fenced lot east of Avenue I reopened for recreational parking, a rigging area
           and ramp maintenance. Get a written commitment from TIDA's new director, Sheela Jivan, before the
           unit-increase approval.
           Oppose any visitor toll, and ask BCDC to review metered parking at shoreline access points against
           the permit's public access requirements.
           Use the unit-increase approval and environmental addendum to lock in launch, rigging and parking
           improvements on the NE and NW shores.
           Ask the State Lands Commission to require TIDA's overdue trust revenue statements.
           Keep the coalition with the Treasure Island Organizing Committee and the Sailing Center active while
           the project is paused.

Plans and documents: Treasure Island Public Trust Exchange Act, 2004 · State Lands Commission title
settlement, 2012 · SFCTA, Treasure Island Transportation Program · TIDA, unit increase item, Feb 2026 ·
SFMTA, Treasure Island project




QQcandlestickQQ




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                      Page 19
QQcandlestickQQ




                                                                         Candlestick Point
                                                                         COMPROMISED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Brisbane council vote, on or after Nov 9, 2026


State Parks lists the park as open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., which ends evening sessions. The access problems the
2025 audit described remain: lost street parking and recurring flooding. The SFBA continues to work
with the Hunters Point community and State Parks.
A development upwind. Brisbane's Baylands plan would allow 1,800 to 2,200 homes and about 6.5 million
square feet of commercial space on the former rail yard and landfill directly upwind of Candlestick Point.
The Planning Commission recommended approval in August 2026, and the council's final vote comes on
or after November 9. This development is outside of the BCDC's jurisdiction.
Windsurfers have warned since at least 2013 that tall buildings on the site could slow the wind at
Candlestick and make it gustier. That year the Candlestick Preservation Association petitioned Brisbane,
arguing that earlier studies did not measure the area sailors actually use. The 2026 Final EIR responds
with a computer wind model by the consultant RWDI, which included Candlestick and measured wind at
the height of a windsurfer's sail. It found the project would cut average wind speeds by 1 to 2 mph about
300 yards downwind, and make the wind near the shore gustier. It concluded that this would not
substantially degrade the wind resource. That conclusion deserves a closer look before the council votes.
At a launch known for its steady breeze, a change that results in less wind and more gusts definitely
qualifies as a degradation of its wind.
Cleaning up the site first. Before anything is built, the Baylands has to be cleaned up, and that work is
under way. At an October 5 meeting of the Brisbane Baylands Community Advisory Group, the Regional
Water Board and the state Department of Toxic Substances Control laid out where it stands:

           What is there. The Brisbane Landfill, used from 1932 to 1967, sits unlined on Bay mud beside Brisbane
           Lagoon, which opens to the Bay a short distance south of Candlestick. The former rail yard holds
           pockets of Bunker C fuel oil, metals and PCBs, and solvents have migrated into its groundwater from
           the Schlage site in San Francisco.
           The plan. About 1.9 million cubic yards of stockpiled soil, in mounds 53 to 78 feet high on the landfill,
           has been tested and will be moved to the rail yard as a clean cap at least five feet thick. The landfill will
           then be closed under a new cap, with a cutoff wall on its east and south sides to keep leachate from
           moving off site. Closure is expected to take 12 to 15 years.
           Water quality. Leachate already seeps toward Brisbane Lagoon and is collected along the landfill's
           southern edge. Stormwater will drain to the Bay through Visitation Creek and restored wetlands. A
           2022 Water Board order requires the landfill to plan for sea level and groundwater rise through 2100




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                    Page 20
             and to update that plan every five years; the next update is due in 2027. The landfill's original waste
             has never been sampled directly, and the check for radioactive material was a records review only.
             Oversight. The Water Board's case manager of 17 years retired this year, and the agency says it is
             short-staffed.

What it means for sailors. Whatever leaves the landfill or the cap ends up in the water we sail on. The
SFBA will keep an eye on the cutoff wall, the stormwater design and the 2027 sea level rise update, and in
making sure the untested legacy waste is characterized before rising groundwater reaches it.
2026–27 priorities:
             Seek extended hours or after-hours access for boardsailors.
             Include Candlestick in State Parks' shoreline resilience planning.
             Review the EIR wind analysis (Appendix O) and comment before the Brisbane council vote on or after
             November 9.
             Follow the Baylands cleanup: attend Brisbane's October 15 council hearing on phasing and
             remediation, comment on the stormwater and Visitation Creek design and the landfill's 2027 sea level
             and groundwater rise update.

Plans and documents: California State Parks, Candlestick Point SRA · City of San Francisco, 2025 Sea
Level Rise Guidance · City of Brisbane, Baylands · Brisbane Baylands 2026 Final EIR · Final EIR Appendix
O, Wind Analysis · Candlestick Preservation Association petition, 2013




QQcrissyQQ




                                                                         Crissy Field
                                                                         THREATENED (MID-TERM)

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Crissy Field Next design and environmental review


Crissy Field is the Bay's signature launch and one of the best-known boardsailing sites in the world. For
many riders, sailing under the Golden Gate Bridge is a bucket-list goal. Over 200 sailors a day often
launch and land at the beach under ideal conditions. In 2026 Crissy hosted the US Wingfoil
Championship for the third year in a row.
The launch is tied to its specific layout. Sailors rig on the turf next to their cars at the west end of the
East Beach lot, then carry their gear barefoot across the Promenade to the beach. The Boardsailing Plan
explains why the west end matters: it is "upwind and west of the rocky riprap shoreline and provides a
sandy and safe area for launching and landing even during a flood tide when sailors are being pushed
toward the rocks to the east." To the west, the Crissy Field Wildlife Protection Area is closed to our users



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                       Page 21
under the park's rules, so East Beach is the only place along Crissy's shore where sailors can launch. The
plan is direct about the corridor between car and water: "Limiting obstructions and interactions
between sailors and other users between the parking area and the beach is critical to maintain safety." By
NPS's 2016 count, the East Beach lot holds 400 vehicles: 178 paved spaces, 156 reinforced turf spaces and
66 event turf spaces. NPS also noted that "Boardsailors prefer to park on the west side of the lot as it
provides them direct access to the best launching locations." Being able to see the water from the lot is a
safety feature too. Riders on the beach spot sailors in trouble and call for help.
That layout has been defended before.
    1993: a draft Presidio plan would have "severely limit[ed] launch access at Crissy Field." Windsurfers
    organized and pushed back.
    2001: the restoration built the turf parking and rigging area that sailors use today.
    2016: NPS proposed to reconfigure the East Beach lot into 367 paved spaces and 33 turf spaces,
    removing most of the rigging turf. NPS received 130 comments, many from boardsailors, and SFBA
    wrote as a park partner since 1986. NPS dropped the reconfiguration: "No reconfiguration of the
    parking lot will occur as part of the proposed project. Future changes to this area will be addressed at
    a separate time through another planning process."

That separate planning process is now under way.
What is coming.
    Sea level rise. The Presidio tide gauge has recorded eight inches of rise over the past century. The
    city's 2025 guidance projects about 0.8 feet by 2050 and 3.1 feet by 2100 under its intermediate
    scenario. USGS rated the Crissy beach "very high" vulnerability in 2005. NPS's own 2016 analysis puts
    minor flooding of the East Beach lot at an 11-foot water level and significant flooding at 12 feet, which
    it equates to 3 feet of sea level rise above today's 100-year tide.
    Rise-Up (2016). A $135,000 Coastal Conservancy grant funded a study by the Parks Conservancy, NPS
    and the Presidio Trust of Crissy under 3-foot and 6-foot sea level rise. It used four strategies: protect,
    retreat (remove infrastructure and restore wetlands), adapt, and access (reroute paths). NPS says it is
    using the results "to help us relocate infrastructure, and to expand riparian and marsh areas to serve
    as a buffer for sea level rise."
    Crissy Field Next. NPS, the Parks Conservancy and the Presidio Trust started this redesign in 2018.
    The lead landscape architects describe future initiatives that include "an expanded tidal marsh
    adapted to 3 feet of sea level rise, and parking improvements," with environmental review and
    implementation to follow. There has been no public update since 2019, but a Haas Jr. Foundation grant
    paid for planning and design work in 2025. No plan has been adopted and no environmental document
    has been released.
    The marsh and the beach are linked. Sand moves east along Crissy at about 25,000 cubic yards a
    year, and the marsh inlet has closed and reopened repeatedly since 2001. A 2004 marsh expansion
    study found that about 32 acres would be needed to keep the marsh open to the tides. It also warned
    that "temporary and long-term changes to the morphology of East Beach are expected following
    wetland expansion." Expanding the marsh could reshape the beach sailors launch from.

The risk. Every adaptation tool on the table touches the corridor that makes the launch work. "Relocate
infrastructure" can mean moving parking away from the west end. "Access" in the planning framework
means rerouting paths, which can put new crossings between the turf and the water. A bigger marsh can



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                   Page 22
change the beach itself. None of the published planning material treats the launch layout as a design
requirement. The new public messaging doesn't mention recreation either. A July 2026 Urban Land
article marking Crissy's 25th anniversary says "resilience doesn't have to mean walls and barriers" and
never mentions sailors.

The decisions will also be made by weakened institutions:
    Jurisdiction. Crissy is federal land. San Francisco's SB 272 shoreline plan does not control it, and
    BCDC's role is limited.
    NPS staffing. The Golden Gate National Recreation Area lost 10 staff in 2025.
    Presidio Trust. A February 2025 executive order directed the Trust to eliminate its non-statutory
    functions, and all six board members were removed in April 2026.
    Funding. Much of the design money is private.

Upkeep is already slipping. Volunteers are chasing the basics:
    Webcam. The East Beach webcam that riders use to check conditions is clouded with moisture.
    Responsibility for it bounced between NPS and the Parks Conservancy for years; it is now confirmed
    as the Conservancy's. The SFBA has asked for a regular maintenance schedule, including cleaning the
    lens and adding desiccant packs to cut moisture.
    No threat to the rigging lawn. In October 2026 NPS confirmed that no current or planned projects
    would affect the East Beach lawn where sailors rig. NPS and the Parks Conservancy are preparing a
    separate project for the airfield and surrounding area, with community engagement expected in the
    coming months; NPS says it will not affect East Beach.
    Shower. The new shower has one nozzle instead of four. NPS has since bought a full replacement and
    plans to install it soon, though no date is set.
    Path work. In September 2026, soil from a path-widening job on the field ended up on the beach and
    in the water. NPS called it a miscommunication and cleaned it up after SFBA reported it.
    Rescue coordination. SFBA runs a volunteer search-and-rescue call tree with the Coast Guard for
    Crissy and the surrounding waters.
    The SFBA checks in with NPS every two weeks on the shower, webcam and other site issues.

Why it matters beyond Crissy. If East Beach loses capacity, San Francisco has no clear substitute:

    Candlestick closes at 7 p.m.
    Treasure Island is closed at 'sunset'.
    Ocean Beach is for advanced riders only.
    Toll Plaza is closed.

Crissy is also a high-profile model for other developments. Parking next to rigging and a clear path to a
sandy launch is exactly what the Golden Gate Fields and Ocean Beach sections ask planners to protect. If
NPS keeps that layout while adapting Crissy to rising seas, it sets a precedent for others.
2026–27 priorities:
    Get the launch layout written into Crissy Field Next as a design requirement before concepts are set:
    west-end parking next to turf rigging;
    a short, unobstructed crossing to the sandy west end of East Beach;
    clear sight lines from the lot to the water;



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                     Page 23
            no net loss of rigging turf or peak-season parking.
            Ask NPS to model how marsh expansion would change East Beach before choosing a design, and to
            manage sand to keep the launch beach.
            Hold NPS to its 2016 commitment that changes to the East Beach lot go through public planning, with
            SFBA at the table as a park partner.
            Get a regular maintenance schedule for the webcam, see the new shower installed, settle who
            maintains the windsock, and formalize SFBA's safety role, including the search-and-rescue call tree
            and docents.
            Keep East Beach parking free.

Plans and documents: Parks Conservancy, Crissy Field Next · CMG, Crissy Field Next · NPS, Adapting to
Climate Change at GGNRA · Crissy Field Marsh Expansion Study, 2004 · NPS, East Beach parking
decision, 2016




QQoceanQQ




                                                                         Ocean Beach
                                                                         THREATENED (MID-TERM)

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Prop G vote, Nov 3, 2026


Ocean Beach is a test-case to see how much the city can let a shoreline move. Managed retreat. What
gets decided here about dunes, sand and access may set the template the Bay's other beaches are
measured against.

What's under the beach. Ocean Beach is also the roof of San Francisco's westside sewer system. Under
the Upper Great Highway, from Lincoln to Sloat, runs the Westside Transport Box, a 20 to 30 foot tall
concrete tube that stores combined sewage and stormwater during heavy rain. South of Sloat, the Lake
Merced Tunnel and the Westside Pump Station carry that flow to the Oceanside treatment plant by the
zoo, and erosion at the south end now threatens the tunnel. The SFPUC puts the cost of moving that
system inland at about $1.6 billion. So the city chose to protect it in place: a $175 million project built
around a 3,200-foot wall buried 55 feet into the beach south of Sloat, covered by reshaped dunes and
kept buried with regular sand management. In short, the plan for sea level rise at OB is driven by the
protection of a critical piece of infrastructure that should have been built elsewhere. Protection of the
Westside Transport Box may cost the city its iconic beach.
The trade-off. A buried wall protects the beach only while it stays buried. Each sand placement costs at
least $1 million. In 2021 a $3.8 million placement was largely gone within months. Once storms expose
the wall, waves reflect off it and scour the sand in front--just take a look at the eroding cliffs and



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                    Page 24
exposed sandbags and riprap at Sloat. Critics, including Surfrider, warn that the beach south of Sloat
could narrow until it disappears at high tide, leaving the city paying for sand indefinitely to protect a
wastewater plant at the expense of a public beach. The Coastal Commission approved the wall as the
only practical way to avoid a sewer failure. Ocean Beach now has both approaches side by side: dunes to
the north, armor to the south.

Where to launch. SFBA recommends launching from the north end of Ocean Beach, at the parking lots
near Kelly's Cove. SFBA does not recommend Sloat. The beach there narrows or disappears at high tide,
riprap and old military concrete line the shore, and the wind turns gusty where the cliffs begin. Few
kiters launch there, so no one is around to help a rider in trouble. SFBA's interest in South Ocean Beach
is in how the plans there shape the whole beach, its sand and the main launch at Kelly's Cove.
The plans in play:

    Ocean Beach Master Plan (SPUR, 2012). In 2018 the city wrote managed retreat into its Local Coastal
    Program. Policy 12.1 adopts managed retreat between Sloat and Skyline, rerouting the Great Highway
    Extension behind the zoo via Sloat and moving beach parking and restrooms out of harm's way. The
    plan has not been updated since 2012.
    SFPUC adaptation project. The Coastal Commission approved a 25-year permit in November 2024 for
    3,200-foot buried wall protecting the Lake Merced Tunnel and wastewater plant, removal of rubble
    and old revetments, a reshaped bluff, a multi-use trail, beach stairs, restrooms and continued sand
    replenishment. . Major construction now starts in late 2029 and runs about four years, and South
    Ocean Beach will likely close about six months of each year during that time. The 35-space lot at Sloat
    will be removed and replaced with about 60 spaces near Skyline.
    SFEI dune management (December 2023). Funded by the Coastal Conservancy, the plan recommends
    rebuilding native dunes from Point Lobos to Sloat, where the SFPUC project takes over, removal of
    iceplant and marram grass, planting beach wildrye, stop grading the backshore at the north end, and
    placing sand cleared from the Great Highway on the beach, where waves can move it, instead of piling
    it behind the beach.
    On the ground. Rec & Park, NPS, SFEI, Surfrider and others began replanting dunes near Judah in
    February 2025 with a $1 million Coastal Conservancy grant. Surfrider reports more than 1,200 native
    plants installed and more than 200 volunteers.
    Sunset Dunes. Voters closed the Upper Great Highway with Prop K in 2024, and it is now Sunset
    Dunes park. A court upheld the closure in January 2026 and an appeal is pending. Prop G, on the
    November 3 ballot, would close the park on weekdays to reopen the Upper Great Highway to cars. An
    SFEI report (October 2024) found that closing the Great Highway to cars has "the greatest and most
    immediate ecological benefits."

Why it matters beyond Ocean Beach. Three things decided here will carry over to other sites.
Resilience vs armor. Ocean Beach is the region's clearest commitment to letting beach and dunes do the
work a seawall would otherwise do, with hard structures only where critical infrastructure needs them.
That is the approach SFBA wants at Crown Beach, where emergency rock is replacing sand, and in every
subregional plan under SB 272.
Sand is a regional supply, and most of it is being sold. USGS researchers found that the mouth of the Bay
lost more than 90 million cubic meters of sediment between 1956 and 2005, and that erosion from
Ocean Beach to Point San Pedro has sped up by about 50% since the 1980s. They tie the loss to a



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                Page 25
shrinking supply of sediment from the Bay. In February 2026 the State Lands Commission renewed
Central Bay sand mining leases for ten years, with a lower cap of 1.395 million cubic yards a year. Its
environmental review found mining is not significantly reducing sand reaching the coast. Baykeeper
sued in March. Meanwhile:

          The Army Corps places about 350,000 cubic yards of shipping-channel sand a year offshore of Ocean
          Beach. An earlier USGS study found the effect of that placement on the beach "largely negligible."
          Alameda's application to put 80,000 cubic yards of sand on its South Shore went unfunded.
          Coastal engineer Bob Battalio, a co-author of the SFEI dune report, notes at an August 26 public
          forum that coarse sand from Bay shoals stays on a beach better than fine windblown sand.

Where the Bay's sand goes, to construction or to our local beaches, decides how much beach our region
keeps.
2026–27 priorities:

          Support the dune-first approach and SFEI's beach sand placement, and ask that both extend along the
          whole beach.
          Ask the city and NPS to designate gear-friendly access points with parking a short carry away,
          including the north parking lots near Kelly's Cove, where kiters launch.
          Ask that the South Ocean Beach project protect sand and access along the whole beach, including the
          north-end launches at Kelly's Cove.
          Ask State Lands, BCDC and the Army Corps to treat recreational beaches, including Ocean Beach and
          Crown Beach, as a priority use for suitable Bay and channel sand, and to put dredged sand on beaches
          where it will stay.
          Ask SPUR and the city to update the 2012 Master Plan with water recreation access as an explicit
          objective.

Plans and documents: SPUR, Ocean Beach Master Plan · SFPUC, Ocean Beach Climate Change
Adaptation Project · SFEI, Growing Resilience (dune management), 2023 · SFEI, Future Opportunities for
the Great Highway, 2024 · Coastal Commission, Western Shoreline Area Plan amendment, 2018




QQthirdaveQQ




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                       Page 26
QQthirdaveQQ




                                                                         3rd Avenue / Baywinds
                                                                         Park, Foster City
                                                                         THREATENED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Baseline memo; final report late spring 2027


3rd Avenue is the Peninsula's main launch and one of the four sites most of the Bay's boardsailors
depend on. It is also the one place where the SFBA is not just defending access but where we're
coordinating work between funders and coastal engineers to do and fund the science to design a resilent
shoreline.
The erosion is long-term and getting worse. The upper beach launch at the north end of Baywinds Park
has been washing away for more than a decade.
          In 2012 the SFBA asked the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation for $500,000 in Cosco Busan oil spill
          settlement funds, with a matching $500,000, to restore and nourish the beach with shell hash. The
          application documented erosion that had already taken much of the upwind launch. It was not funded.
          In 2017 the Bay Area Water Trail described the beach as "rapidly eroding" and warned that "if nothing
          is done, the beach may be gone in the next several years."
          SFEI's 2020 study of eroding Bay shorelines found that beaches need a steady supply of coarse
          sediment, and that falling sediment supply leaves them less able to keep up with rising seas. How
          much wave energy reaches 3rd Avenue, and from which direction, is one of the questions the current
          study is designed to answer.

The levee protects the city, not the beach. Foster City finished its $90 million levee project in February
2024. The new wall is about six feet higher on average and is designed for the 100-year flood with 3 feet
of sea level rise. It holds the line behind the beach but does nothing to keep sand in front of it.
What the SFBA has done. The SFBA has carried this project for years with little public help.
          2019–20: ESA prepared a proposal for a 3rd Avenue habitat, beach and water access restoration
          project. The SFBA set up fiscal sponsorship through Community Initiatives, a 501(c)(3), so private
          donors could fund it.
          2021–24: The project stalled. In November 2024 the City Manager gave the project permission to study
          the city-owned shoreline.
          2025: Private philanthropy funded a comprehensive study by ESA. The SFBA added $20,000 for
          independent technical oversight by coastal engineer Bob Battalio. SFBA board member Ben Botkin
          serves as Project Director.
          2026: The SFBA posted the $5,000 performance bond Foster City required for the encroachment
          permit, and fieldwork began.




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                  Page 27
Why we are measuring wave and tidal energy. A shoreline that protects the launch has to be designed
for the forces that are destroying it. The options on the table are nature-based:
             a nourished beach of coarse sand, gravel or shell that holds against waves;
             offshore oyster reefs or eelgrass beds that take energy out of the waves before they reach the beach;
             a reshaped shoreline that moves with the tides instead of a hard edge that reflects wave energy.

Each of these depends on numbers no one has for this site: how big the waves are and where they come
from, how much energy reaches the shore at each stage of the tide, what the bottom is made of, and
how much sand moves and where. Elsewhere in the Bay, the oyster and eelgrass pilot off San Rafael cut
wave energy by about 30%, and Marin's Aramburu Island beach of gravel, sand and shell has held a
shoreline that had retreated more than 130 feet in 45 years. Those results came from projects designed
for their own sites.
The study collects that data:

             Spotter buoy: a SOFAR Spotter buoy measuring waves, wind and weather for a full year;
             Sediment: samples of the shoreline and nearshore sediment;
             Geotechnical: a review of the ground beneath the shoreline;
             Surveys: vessel-mounted bathymetry and drone lidar of the shoreline profile.

ESA will turn the data into a baseline-conditions memo and then a final report with conceptual design
options, expected in late spring 2027. Local coastal scientists have told the project team it is the first
effort of its kind in the Bay to address shoreline erosion and sea level rise ahead of time with a living-
shoreline design.
Why it matters beyond Foster City. If the upper beach goes, the Peninsula has nowhere else to put
those sailors. Coyote Point, the nearest alternative, is smaller and has its own issues.
The site has the potential to become a model for planning and implementing nature-based solutions to
address shoreline erosion impacts to access. Support from local jurisdictions and regulators, and
significant additional funding, will be required for successful implementation.
2026–27 priorities:
             Complete the study and share the baseline data with Foster City, San Mateo, OneShoreline and BCDC.
             Ask Foster City to start its SB 272 shoreline plan, jointly with San Mateo if possible, and to name the
             Baywinds shoreline as a priority project in it.
             Ask the Regional Water Board and BCDC where the sea level rise adaptation plans required by the
             levee permits stand.
             Line up a public agency sponsor before the final report, so the design can move straight into Measure
             AA, OPC and Coastal Conservancy funding rounds.
             Build a habitat component (oyster reef, eelgrass or dune) into the design so it qualifies for Measure
             AA.

Plans and documents: Foster City Levee Improvements Project · BCDC, local sea level rise plans (SB 272)
· Water Trail, Baywinds Park · SFEI, New Life for Eroding Shorelines

                                                                         Coyote Point
                                                                         COMPROMISED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         San Mateo County Parks repair of the retaining wall


While Boardsports reports no pressing access issue at the Coyote Point launch, it does report a safety
problem. The western promenade rock retaining wall built in 2013–14 keeps flushing small rocks onto the
beach and into the water, and the foot of the wall is failing. That is the responsibility of San Mateo
County Parks.
2026–27 priorities:

             Ask San Mateo County Parks to repair the failing retaining wall.




QQsanquentinQQ




                                                                         San Quentin /
                                                                         Windsurfer Beach
                                                                         COMPROMISED

                                                                         N E X T M I L E S TO N E
                                                                         Prison management engagement


In March 2025 the prison began enforcing parking restrictions at the West Gate area that boardsailors
used for decades. The remodel continues. The east-side launch has fewer than 10 spaces and a two-hour
limit.
A Bay Trail project along the launch. Marin County Public Works is designing the East Sir Francis Drake
Bay Trail Gap Closure, a 0.6-mile bike and pedestrian connection between Andersen Drive at I-580 and
Remillard Park in Larkspur, the stretch of road that runs past Windsurfer Beach. It would be either a
multi-use path or a sidewalk with protected bike lanes. Planning and design began in May 2025 with a
$700,000 federal earmark, the county held a public workshop on January 29, 2026, and near-term "quick
build" improvements are being designed. Final design and construction are not yet funded. Sailors
currently park along the shoulder and reach the beach by rough steps cut into the bank.




SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                                         Page 29
2026–27 priorities:
           Establish whether the public has a right of access to the shoreline here.
           Resume contact with prison management as construction winds down.
           Work with Marin County Public Works on the East Sir Francis Drake gap closure so the design keeps
           shoulder parking for the launch and builds safe access down to the beach.

Plans and documents: Marin County, East Sir Francis Drake Blvd Bikeway Gap Closure · Marin County,
workshop notice, Jan 2026 · Marin County Bicycle Coalition, project page and map




QQAquiQQ




A quick overview of our legal framework for access
The public's right to reach the Bay rests on several overlapping layers of law. Agencies tend to cite the
narrowest one.

           California Constitution, Article X.
           Section 4 bars any individual, partnership or corporation holding frontage on navigable waters from
           excluding the public's right of way to that water when it is needed for a public purpose. It directs that
           the provision be construed so that access "shall be always attainable for the people."
           Section 3 withholds tidelands within two miles of a city from sale to private parties.
           The public trust. Much of the Bay shoreline, including Berkeley's waterfront and Treasure Island, is
           tideland held in trust for the public. Cities that hold granted tidelands must file an annual statement
           of trust revenues and expenditures with the State Lands Commission (Public Resources Code §6306).
           Berkeley's filings give only generalized totals, without the detail that would show how much marina
           money is going to park maintenance and recreation programs. The Commission has not required
           more.
           The McAteer-Petris Act and BCDC jurisdiction. BCDC's permit authority covers the Bay itself and a
           100-foot shoreline band. Under 14 CCR §10131, the Bay Plan maps "do not establish the extent of the
           Commission's jurisdiction": the statute and regulations control. Where fill history is uncertain, as
           BCDC's own staff say it is at Berkeley, jurisdiction is a question of fact.
           San Francisco Bay Plan policies.
           Public access policy calls for "maximum feasible access to and along the waterfront" in every new
           shoreline development.
           Recreation Policy 3 calls for recreational facilities to be "easily available from parking reserved for the
           public." It also calls for "sufficient, convenient parking" at launch sites for non-motorized small boats.
           Recreation Policy 9 allows ferry terminals in waterfront parks only where they do not interfere with
           recreation. It adds that park and marina parking "should not be usurped by ferry patrons."
           Bay Plan Map 4 directs Berkeley to "preserve marina, beach, small boat launch, windsurfing access,
           fishing pier."
           BCDC's environmental justice policies call for engagement with, and mitigation for, affected
           communities.
           The San Francisco Bay Area Water Trail Act. It declares that non-motorized water recreation,
           sailboarding included, is "of great benefit to the public welfare."



SFBA · The State of Recreational Access to The San Francisco Bay: 2026                                           Page 30
            The Regional Shoreline Adaptation Plan. BCDC adopted it on December 5, 2024. Under SB 272, every
            shoreline city and county must adopt a subregional adaptation plan consistent with it by January 1,
            2034. These plans will define the shape of the shoreline, and of access to it, for decades. They are the
            most important venue for recreation over the next eight years.




QQ2026–QQ




2026–27 priorities
1. Berkeley. Discourage the BCDC from permitting paid-parking at this park. Insist that the ferry project
   be judged on real use data, a costed in-marina alternative and a full fiscal accounting.
2. Crown Beach. Get access designed into this winter's storm response. Secure permanent ramps and
   sand before April.
3. Measure use. Build a replicable method for measuring recreational demand from anonymized mobility
   data, starting with Berkeley and Racetrack. Offer it to BCDC and to every subregional plan.
4. Write recreation into the subregional plans. Propose access performance standards for Richmond,
   the East Bay Crescent, Alameda and Foster City: usable beach width, a usable tidal window, launch and
   landing space, and parking prioritized for recreation.
5. Beaches over armor. Where protection is needed, favor sand nourishment and living shorelines. Insist
   that any armoring include designed access through it. Push for a regional sand budget that puts
   suitable Bay and channel sand on recreational beaches.
6. New parkland. Encourage planners to design with regional, not site-specific, goals.
7. Fund the work. Continue to fund and support site-improvement commitment. Find a public sponsor
   for 3rd Avenue. Continue to build the coalition of swimmers, paddlers, anglers and families with
   whom we share our beaches.
